newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ pilots lose appeal to limit use of "black box".
newsitem.headline: NZ pilots lose appeal to limit use of "black box".

text.p: New Zealand's court of appeal on Monday rejected a challenge by the country's airline pilots' union and cleared the way for "black box" voice recordings to be published and released to police investigating a fatal crash.
The case stemmed from the crash two years ago of an Ansett Dash 8 airplane near Palmerston North, on North Island, killing four people and seriously injuring 14.

Police have said they are considering whether the two surviving pilots should be charged with criminal offences relating to the accident. The court ruled they could now apply for a search warrant to access the contents of the recording devices.

The New Zealand Air Line Pilots Association (ALPA) had argued that the 1944 Chicago Convention should prevent cockpit voice recorder data being used for purposes other than preventing further similar accidents.
The pilots have also taken separate proceedings with New Zealand's privacy commissioner to try to protect their rights.

At the same hearing, investigators from the Transport Accident Investigation Commission (TAIC) said they wanted to publish an edited transcript of the recording -- of cockpit voices and some instruments -- in their report into the crash.
The appeal judges also ruled in their favour, and a TAIC spokesman told reporters afterwards that the commission now expected its report to be published by early July.

ALPA said in a statement that it felt the ruling confirmed its belief that, "New Zealand lacks adequate law to protect the use of devices intended only for the reconstruction of accidents for the purposes of preventing further similar ones".
It added that in view of the likely action by police, it would not state a more comprehensive viewpoint "for some time".

However, commenting on the case, TAIC chief executive John Britton told New Zealand Radio he had only sought to publish a transcript for safety reasons, noting it contained only about half the data from the 30 minutes or so leading up to impact.

"We are safety investigators and just as in other countries...(our) investigation has a completely different focus to police investigation, and the evidence is not normally provided by safety investigators to the police," Britton said.
He said TAIC, as an independent agency, had in this case sought to balance the public interest of the flight industry world wide with issues of confidentiality.
The pilots did not say if they might pursue one final avenue of appeal through the Privy Council in London.
